facts.text: Sean Giambrone, the voice of Russell the terrier, is best known as young Adam Goldberg on the long-running sitcom The Goldbergs.
Sports site Extra Mustard (SI) greeted the film in 2014 as the Air Bud creators' leap from dogs playing sports to dogs doing pro wrestling.
Star David Milchard (Nate) said the crew did an incredible job building this vintage wrestling arena for the film.
Director Robert Vince has had a hand in producing every film in the Air Bud family, from the original golden retriever hit to the Buddies sequels and the primate movies.
Fred Willard, voicing wrestling announcer TJ, was cast in a clueless sports-announcer role; Swampflix noted he's basically reprising his Best in Show commentator.
Co-star David Milchard said it was cool working with the same monkey as Ben Stiller, Zach Galifianakis and Bradley Cooper.
Hunk is played by Crystal the Monkey, who also appeared in the Night at the Museum films and The Hangover Part II. Will Sasso supplies the voice.
Star David Milchard (Nate) said the animal trainers left everyone on set in awe, joking you'll never be more charming than any of these animals.
Swampflix noted this is the first Air Bud Entertainment film without Air Bud's puppies; their earlier Air Buddies movies went straight to DVD.
Spectrum Culture's Pat Padua wrote the film's 1980s-style wrestling world is every bit as ridiculous as the Iron Sheik vs. Sgt. Slaughter rivalry, and he liked the dry-ice entrances.
Fandango premiered the trailer exclusively on December 5, 2014, and booked the film into theaters on February 21, 2015 as part of its Family Screening Series.
Only about 4-6 different shots of Hunk the monkey are used in the whole film. They were slowed, sped up and recut to make him seem to do more, saving money.
Swampflix's Brandon Ledet noted the title Russell Madness is never spoken; he's called Russell Mania, and Ledet guessed the change dodges WWE's WrestleMania brand.
Swampflix's Brandon Ledet counted Russell's foes: a mummy, a caveman, a pirate, a clown, an escaped convict and a California surfer. Basically a wrestling-gimmick parade.
Wrestling boss Mick Vaughn is played by John Ratzenberger (Cliff on Cheers). Swampflix's Brandon Ledet calls the character a Vince McMahon-style villain.
Swampflix's Brandon Ledet read Mick Vaughn's Wrestlers United Federation as a WWF/WWE stand-in swallowing local promotions, and lined the film up with Body Slam and No Holds Barred.
The theme song 'Maniac' was written by Gregory Prechel and Brahm Wenger, who also wrote the closing 'You Can Make It'.
Director Robert Vince began directing in 2000 with MVP: Most Valuable Primate, a sports comedy starring a hockey-playing chimp.
The Hammer is played by John Hennigan, better known as WWE's John Morrison. Wrestling Inc. covered the trailer in 2015 as him wrestling a dog.
The film gets a shout-out in the 2022 movie Diary of a Wimpy Kid.
Spectrum Culture's Pat Padua singled out the dry-ice fog entrances as a detail where the movie gets real wrestling spectacle right.
David Milchard (Nate) watched wrestling as a kid, so working on the arena set was a dream. He said it was a shame when the set was torn down after filming.
Filming took place in New Westminster, British Columbia, even though the story is set in Portland.
John Hennigan (The Hammer, ex-WWE's John Morrison) said wrestling and movies are the two things he finds most fulfilling creatively.
Swampflix's Brandon Ledet wrote in May 2015 that Russell Madness might become his favorite bad movie of the year.
Theatrically it barely registered: Box Office Mojo lists just $43,288 worldwide, all from Peru, with a widest release of 10 theaters.
Common Sense Media's Renee Longstreet wrote it can't live up to the original Air Bud and is unlikely to become a family classic, though it can make kids laugh.
After a limited run, 20th Century Fox put it out on Blu-ray and DVD on March 10, 2015. The Numbers estimates about $1.12 million in domestic video sales.
Spectrum Culture's Pat Padua noted director Robert Vince has directed nine of the 14 Air Bud franchise titles, most of them direct to video.
DVD Talk's Randy Miller III called it a total misfire, said the acting is Z-grade Disney Channel bad, and gave it a Skip It.
Pat Padua of Spectrum Culture gave the film 3 out of 5. Common Sense Media gave it 2 stars.
The faith-and-family site Dove.org gave it its Family-Approved Seal for all ages; reviewer Donna Rolfe praised the family-first message.
